verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster. Of the servant of YHWH. Of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the leader of the singers. A song of a servant of the LORD. Of David.
verses.directors_commentary: The superscription is not part of the poem's story, but it frames how it must be spoken. Hebrew has only two words for the speaker: 'servant of YHWH' and 'of David'. KJV expands this into 'A Psalm of David the servant of the Lord', which turns an identification into a title and drops the line break between them. In Hebrew, 'servant of YHWH' stands alone as the psalmist's stance: he is a man who has a master, and the rest of the psalm is about a wicked man who says he has none (Radak). Pronounce it as a credential. Compare the same title for Moses (Deut 34:5) and Joshua (Josh 24:29): in the ancient Near East 'servant of' was a court title as much as a humility formula, as in the seals of royal officials. 'Of David' (לְדָוִד) is the usual lamed of attribution, 'belonging to' or 'for', and does not by itself say who wrote it. The choirmaster (מְנַצֵּחַ) is the Temple musical overseer; the root is נצח 'to excel, to be over', and KJV's 'chief Musician' is acceptable.

philological_notes.note: 'Servant of YHWH' as a standing title of loyalty, set against the wicked man who has no fear of God. Radak reads it as marking the psalmist as truly God's servant, who knows he has a master who rewards good and evil.

verses.translation_literal: [The] utterance of Transgression to the wicked [is] in the midst of my heart: there is no fear of God before his eyes.
verses.translation_dramatic: A voice speaks, and I hear it in the deep of my own heart: Transgression itself, murmuring to the wicked man. There is no dread of God. Nothing stands before his eyes to make him tremble.
verses.directors_commentary: This opening is the hardest line of the psalm, and the actors need to know it is meant to puzzle. נְאֻם is the word of prophetic oracle, 'utterance of YHWH' elsewhere (Isa 1:24, as Metzudat Zion notes), and here it is given to Transgression itself, as though Sin were a false prophet speaking to the wicked man. The preposition ל 'to' is the pressure point: 'the utterance of Transgression to the wicked' is a speech addressed to him. And where is it heard? 'In the midst of my heart' (בְּקֶרֶב לִבִּי) is the psalmist's own inner ear: he overhears the voice, as Rashi says, 'it seems to me', and Radak that Transgression, the evil impulse, speaks. KJV flattens this into 'The transgression of the wicked saith within my heart': it turns the oracle into a verb ('saith'), drops the 'to', and so makes the wicked man's own sin the speaker. BBE goes further and moves the heart to 'his heart', following LXX and Syriac, which smooths the oddity at the cost of the Hebrew. The line ends with the content of the voice: 'no fear of God before his eyes'. Pachad is not polite reverence but dread, the shudder that stops a hand; 'before his eyes' is the visible horizon of conduct. The wicked man has nothing in his line of sight that can frighten him. Play it low and close, as a dark whisper the speaker can't unhear.

philological_notes.note: The oracle formula, normally 'utterance of YHWH'. Its use for the voice of Transgression is deliberate irony: Sin speaks as an inverted prophet.
'Transgression', in the sense of rebellion against a lord. The commentators identify it with the evil impulse and compare Gen 4:7 'sin crouches at the door'.
Dread, a trembling fear, not reverent respect. 'No dread of God' means the sense of being answerable has gone.

verses.translation_literal: For he has made smooth to himself in his eyes, to find his iniquity, to hate [it].
verses.translation_dramatic: For he has smoothed the road before his own eyes, soothing himself until his guilt is never found, never named, never hated.
verses.directors_commentary:
Every English version is guessing at this verse, because the Hebrew is two bare infinitives hanging off a verb. הֶחֱלִיק is 'made smooth', the root of חֲלָקוֹת 'smooth words', the oiled phrase of the flatterer (Prov 2:16, 28:23). Here the wicked man smooths over his own conscience 'in his own eyes' (בְּעֵינָיו), the same eyes that held no dread of God in v.2, and the same Transgression that spoke to him there is now the one whose talk he finds so smooth.

Then: 'to find his iniquity, to hate'. KJV and Webster read it as a limit, 'until his iniquity be found to be hateful', which adds a clause of time the Hebrew does not have. ASV and BBE read it as the wicked man's confidence that his iniquity 'will not be found out and be hated'. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David take it as the purpose of the smoothing: so that God finds his iniquity and hates it. Radak gives a different reading: 'to find' means to search out the evil deed until he finds it (as in 1 Sam 20:21, 'go, find the arrows'), and 'to hate' means to hate the good way, as 'they left the LORD to keep' means to keep other gods (Hos 4:10). Meiri has the same two options. The literal layer keeps the bare infinitives so every reading stays open. For the actor, the working sense is a conscience so well oiled that the sin slides past unseen. 'To find' (לִמְצֹא) and 'to hate' (לִשְׂנֹא) end in the same sound, two short hard stops.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of חלק II 'be smooth': to make smooth, to flatter, to soothe. Here reflexive ('to himself'): self-flattery, the smoothing of his own conscience. KJV 'flattereth himself' has the sense and lacks the image of slickness.

Two bare infinitives of purpose or result. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David: so that God finds his iniquity and hates it. Radak and Meiri: he seeks out the evil deed until he finds it, and hates the good way. The ambiguity is part of the verse.

verses.translation_literal: The words of his mouth [are] mischief and deceit; he has ceased to act wisely, to do good.
verses.translation_dramatic: The words of his mouth are trouble and treachery. He has stopped being wise. He has stopped doing good.
verses.directors_commentary: Now the voice of the wicked man becomes audible, and it is rotten. אָוֶן is not just 'iniquity' (KJV, ASV): it is trouble, trouble-making, the empty and harmful thing, and Metzudat Zion glosses it 'toil and falsehood'. מִרְמָה is deceit, the tricking tongue of Ps 5:7 and 10:7. The pair is a hendiadys for lying speech that causes harm. 'He has ceased' (חָדַל) is the same verb used for a worker laying down tools, and with a following infinitive, as Ibn Ezra and Meiri point out, it works like 'they ceased to build the city' (Gen 11:8). KJV 'he hath left off to be wise' is archaic but right. The nuance is in הִשְׂכִּיל: not abstract wisdom, but the insight that makes things go well, practical prudence. The wicked man hasn't just made a bad choice; he has abandoned the habit that would let him make a good one (Malbim, Rashi). 'To do good' (לְהֵיטִיב) belongs to the same verb: stop acting wisely, stop acting well. A good actor should flatten the voice on 'ceased'. Two short falling words, no drama.

philological_notes.note: Trouble, harm, mischief, emptiness. Not just moral 'iniquity': the word covers the empty and harmful. Metzudat Zion glosses it 'toil and falsehood'.
'He has ceased' followed by an infinitive, as in Gen 11:8 'they ceased to build'. הִשְׂכִּיל is practical insight, the wisdom that leads to success.

verses.translation_literal: Mischief he plans on his bed; he takes his stand on a way [that is] not good; evil he does not reject.
verses.translation_dramatic: On his own bed, in the dark, he plans mischief. By day he plants his feet on a road that is not good. Evil he does not spurn.
verses.directors_commentary: Three short clauses, three stages: night, day, and the verdict. The bed (מִשְׁכָּב) is the place where a man is alone with his thoughts, 'when he turns aside from his business' (Metzudat David, Radak); Mic 2:1 uses the same image ('woe to those who devise iniquity and work evil upon their beds'). It is the opposite of Ps 4:5 and 63:7, where the righteous reflect on God upon the bed. Then 'he takes his stand' (יִתְיַצֵּב): the verb is the one for taking a position, planting oneself, as a soldier or a witness does. KJV's 'setteth himself in a way' is fine; the sense is that he is no longer drifting but stationed. 'Not good' (לֹא טוֹב) is a litotes, a deliberate understatement, like 'a not-good balance' in Prov 20:23; Radak counts the parallels and also offers the avoidance of saying 'evil' twice. KJV's 'abhorreth' for יִמְאָס is strong: the Hebrew 'reject, spurn' is the verb for turning something down, and the wicked man is the one who never turns evil down. The final clause is an understated, almost flat close: he does not refuse. Play it cold.

philological_notes.note: 'On his bed', the place of private reflection. The same image is used in Mic 2:1 and reversed for the righteous in Ps 4:5 and 63:7.
'Not good', an understatement that means 'bad'. Radak lists parallels (Isa 65:2, Ezek 18:18, Prov 20:23).
To reject, spurn, refuse. KJV 'abhorreth' is stronger than the Hebrew: the point is that he never turns evil away.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, in the heavens [is] your covenant loyalty; your faithfulness [is] to the clouds.
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD, your steadfast love fills the heavens. Your faithfulness climbs to the clouds.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poem turns here, and the voice must turn with it: after four verses of low, close, private whispering, the camera lifts to the sky. Meiri and Malbim treat the verse as the answer to the wicked man's 'there is no fear of God': God's loyalty is not absent but vast, and Metzudat David likewise says the truth is that God's loyalty reaches from earth to heaven. Rashi reads it the other way: because of such wicked men, you withdraw kindness from those below and lift your faithfulness to the skies, away from the sons of men. Both readings stand on the same words; the verse's setting after vv.2-5 favours the answer.

חֶסֶד is the hardest Hebrew word to carry: covenant loyalty, the faithful action owed and given inside a bond. KJV's 'mercy' is too weak and makes it a pardon; ASV 'lovingkindness' is closer. אֱמוּנָה is faithfulness, reliability, firmness. Both verbs are missing: 'in the heavens', 'to the clouds'. Radak and Metzudat Zion say 'in the heavens' (בְּהַשָּׁמַיִם, with the article, irregular after the preposition) means 'up to the heavens', as in Lam 4:14, and that heavens and clouds are one parallel, as in Ps 57:11. The scale is measured by height because the wicked man has set his sights low, at his bed and his road. Ancient listeners knew the heavens as the place of the storm god; here YHWH fills them. Speak it slow and wide, with space between the words.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty: faithful action within a bond. 'Mercy' (KJV) hears only the forgiveness.
The article after בְּ is irregular. Radak and Metzudat Zion take it as 'unto the heavens', parallel to 'to the clouds'. The root is the noun שָׁמַיִם 'heavens'.

verses.translation_literal: Your righteousness [is] like [the] mountains of God; your judgments [are] [the] great deep. Human and beast you deliver, YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your righteousness stands like the mountains of God. Your judgments lie deep as the great deep. Human and beast alike, O LORD, you bring through.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two images of scale, then a surprise. 'Mountains of God' (הַרְרֵי־אֵל) uses God's name as a superlative: Radak compares 'a great city to God' (Jonah 3:3) and 'cedars of God' (Ps 80:11), so KJV's 'great mountains' catches the sense and loses the divine name, which the Hebrew hears as 'mountains as only God could set them'. The mountains are high and fixed; the deep (תְּהוֹם) is the primeval ocean of Gen 1:2, unreachable below the earth. Between them they span the whole cosmos, height to depth. Ibn Ezra reads both as unfathomable to man; Radak and Metzudat David read the mountains as the refuge God gives the good, and the deep as where the wicked sink. Ancient listeners would feel the mountain of the gods and the abyss as the two places of divine power.

Then the surprise: 'human and beast you deliver'. KJV's 'preservest' is right; יָשַׁע is 'to save, to bring out of a tight place'. The commentators divide on what the pairing means. Metzudat David and Meiri: God's care covers every creature, though Meiri calls it care for the kind, not the individual. Ibn Ezra: he judges every sentient being. Radak: the kindness God shows even the wicked is like the kindness he shows the beast that does not know him, for the wicked is a beast in human form. Malbim: man has a bodily part like the beast's and a rational part that is human. Drop your voice on 'beast' with a kind of wonder.

philological_notes.note: 'Mountains of God': אֵל as intensifier, 'towering mountains'. Compare 'a great city to God' (Jonah 3:3) and 'cedars of God' (Ps 80:11).
The 'great deep', the primeval ocean (Gen 1:2, 7:11). 'Great' here has weight, not just size.
To deliver, to bring out of tight places. KJV 'preservest' is fine; the verb normally describes rescue, which is more than keeping.

verses.translation_literal: How precious [is] your covenant loyalty, God! And [the] sons of humankind in [the] shadow of your wings take refuge.
verses.translation_dramatic: How precious is your steadfast love, O God! And the children of humankind run to shelter in the shadow of your wings.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalm turns from the cosmos to a close-up. The speaker is not describing a doctrine; he is exclaiming. מַה is the exclamatory 'how!', and יָקָר is 'precious, rare, costly', the word used of precious stones (1 Kings 5:17, 10:2). KJV's 'excellent' is vague, and its 'therefore the children of men put their trust' inserts a causal link the Hebrew does not have: it is simply 'and', so refuge follows the exclamation as a second thought. 'Sons of humankind' (בְּנֵי אָדָם) is the ordinary phrase for people in general, picking up the 'human' of v.7. Rashi and Radak restrict it to the righteous, those who are truly human and not beast-like; the words themselves name humankind.

The image of wings is a mother bird's: the ancient Near East also pictured a deity under a winged sun disk, and the Temple's cherubim spread their wings over the ark. 'Take refuge' (חָסָה) is the standard verb of fleeing to a protector; KJV 'put their trust' loses the physical running-in. Say it with warmth, and let the verb breathe: they take refuge, and they are still taking it.

philological_notes.note: Precious, costly, rare: the word for jewels. KJV 'excellent' loses the sense of value.
'In the shadow of your wings': a mother bird sheltering chicks, and perhaps the cherubim's wings over the ark. The image also occurs in Ps 17:8, 57:2 and 63:8.
Take refuge: to run to a protector. The final nun is an older imperfect ending, also seen in 'they take their fill' (v.9); my own grammatical reading.

verses.translation_literal: They take their fill from the fatness of your house, and [the] river of your delights you give them to drink.
verses.translation_dramatic: They eat and are full from the richness of your house, and you pour them drink from the river of your delights.
verses.directors_commentary: The refuge becomes a banquet. 'Your house' (בֵּיתֶךָ) is the Temple, and the 'fatness' (דֶּשֶׁן) is the rich portion of the sacrifice: in the ancient Near East meat was rare, and the fat of the offering was the best part, given to the gods and shared out in the festive meal. Jer 31:14 uses the same word for the priests' 'fatness' and Ps 63:6 for the soul 'satisfied as with marrow and fat'. KJV's 'abundantly satisfied' catches the verb יִרְוְיֻן, which is 'drenched, watered through' (the root רוה is the soaked ground, as in Isa 55:10), so the first verb is already a drink image before the second arrives. 'Delights' is עֲדָנֶיךָ, from the root of 'Eden': KJV's 'pleasures' loses the sound of the garden, and the commentators (Metzudat David) hear in 'river' the river that went out from Eden (Gen 2:10). It is a hearing, not a proof, but the audience would have caught it. Note the change of person: the 'they' of humankind is now the guests, and the 'you' of God is the host who serves and pours. Warm, low, unhurried.

philological_notes.note: Fatness, the rich portion of a sacrifice and of a feast. The best part, shared at the Temple meal.
Delights, from the root also heard in 'Eden'. The commentators read 'river' as a hint of Eden's river; this is a resonance, not a settled link.

verses.translation_literal: For with you [is] a fountain of life; in your light we see light.
verses.translation_dramatic: For with you is the spring of life itself, and in your light we see light.
verses.directors_commentary: The reason beneath the banquet, said as plainly as a creed. מָקוֹר is a spring, a source, not a stored water: Radak and Metzudat Zion both stress 'a flowing well' as against the cistern that runs dry (Jer 2:13 sets the 'fountain of living waters' against 'broken cisterns'). 'With you' (עִמְּךָ) is not 'from you': the life is kept beside God, at his side, and one must come near. 'Life' in Hebrew is plural (חַיִּים), the usual plural of fullness. The second clause is a pun that English does well and KJV has kept: 'in your light we see light' is bə'orkha nir'eh 'or, with 'or twice, so that the light itself is the thing that makes light visible. Ibn Ezra and Radak hear in it the reward of the world to come; Malbim hears a spiritual light by which ordinary light is seen. Whichever, no one in the ancient world saw anything without daylight, and the fire and the sun were gifts; here the sun is only a spark of something else. Say 'light' the second time softer, as if surprised.

philological_notes.note: A spring of life: flowing, not stored, water. Compare Prov 14:27 and Jer 2:13.
The repeated word 'or 'light' is the pun: light is only seen by light. Commentators read it as the light of the world to come (Ibn Ezra, Radak) or of the mind (Malbim).

verses.translation_literal: Draw out your covenant loyalty to those who know you, and your righteousness to [the] upright of heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: Keep drawing out your steadfast love for those who know you, and your righteousness for the upright of heart.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns to petition, and the first word is a physical image. מְשֹׁךְ is 'draw, pull out', as one pulls a rope or a bowstring, or lengthens a note; Radak compares 'he extended kindness to him' (Gen 39:21) and 'I have drawn you with loyalty' (Jer 31:3). KJV 'O continue' keeps the duration and loses the pull: the speaker wants God's loyalty stretched out like thread, long enough to reach the people who need it. Radak and Meiri hear a prayer for this world, that those who know God may be free to study and keep his commandments; Radak allows the world to come as well.

'Those who know you' (לְיֹדְעֶיךָ) is the Hebrew 'know' of relationship, as in 'knew his wife', not information. 'Upright of heart' (יִשְׁרֵי־לֵב) is the exact opposite of the wicked man of vv.2-3: he is the one to whom Transgression speaks and who flatters himself in his own eyes, while these are straight inside, with nothing to smooth over. The two halves pair loyalty with the knowing, righteousness with the upright. Say it as a request from someone who knows how this could go wrong. The imperative is polite, not a demand: from a servant to a master it carries the weight of trust, not of command.

philological_notes.note: Draw out, prolong, extend: the image is pulling a thread or a rope. KJV 'continue' keeps the sense of duration but not the pull.
'Those who know you': the verb of relationship and acknowledgement, not only of information.

verses.translation_literal: May [the] foot of pride not come to me, and [the] hand of [the] wicked not make me wander.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let no foot of pride come near me, and let no hand of the wicked drive me from my place.
verses.directors_commentary:
A prayer of protection, and the speaker uses two body parts: the foot that tramples and the hand that pushes. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David read 'the foot of pride' (רֶגֶל גַּאֲוָה) as proud enemies coming to attack him, 'with foot and with hand' as Radak says, one marching, one fighting. Rashi reads it differently: let not the foot of these wicked men come with me at the time of reward, to share a portion with the righteous. Malbim hears intellectual pride. KJV 'come against me' is a good gloss on תְּבוֹאֵנִי, which with the object suffix means 'come upon me', as in 'let ruin come upon him' (Ps 35:8, cited by Radak). The verb is feminine, because 'foot' is feminine; so is the verb of the hand.

'Remove me' (תְּנִדֵנִי) is from נוּד, 'to wander, to flee, to shake': being shoved out of one's place and made a wanderer, as Cain was a 'nod' (Gen 4:12, 14). KJV 'remove' is too tame; ASV 'drive me away' catches the force. The wicked man of v.5 'takes his stand'; now the speaker asks that no wicked foot stand over him. Say it quietly, without bravado. The request is answered in the next breath, in v.13.

philological_notes.note: The foot of pride, which tramples. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David: proud enemies coming to attack. Rashi: the wicked coming to share the righteous man's reward. Malbim: intellectual pride.
From נוד 'wander, flee, be shaken'. Compare Cain's wandering (Gen 4:12, 14). 'Remove' (KJV) is too tame; the sense is driving out of one's place.

verses.translation_literal: There they have fallen, doers of iniquity; they were pushed down, and they were not able to rise.
verses.translation_dramatic: There, right there, they have fallen, the makers of mischief, the ones who laboured at wrong. Thrust down, and thrust down hard. They strain to stand, and they cannot rise.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play the first word as a pointing finger. Nobody in the verse says where 'there' is, and that is the point: the poet has just prayed that the foot of pride and the hand of the wicked not drive him away (v.12), and now he sees the spot. Ibn Ezra reads it as the place where they planned to dislodge him, and also as an echo of the fate of earlier wrongdoers; Metzudat David reads it as the place where they come to press him. Malbim takes 'there' to be the world to come. Ibn Ezra and Meiri also compare it to 'then', as in Job 35:12. The Hebrew allows each, so give the word weight and leave it open.

The verb is a perfect, 'they have fallen', though the scene lies ahead. Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all call this a past form standing for the future, the way prophecy speaks of a thing as already done. Play it as certainty, not as a report: the singer has already seen it. The KJV's 'There are the workers of iniquity fallen' uses the archaic English perfect ('are fallen'), which matches the Hebrew perfect and carries the same sense of a finished fall. 'Workers of iniquity' is the old stock phrase for pō'ălê 'āwen, 'doers of trouble', a person who makes wrongdoing his trade. 'Āwen is not an abstract 'iniquity' but trouble, harm and emptiness together, and it is the word the psalm used in vv.4 and 5 for the wicked man's speech and plans.

The verbs run in three steps: they fell, they were pushed down, they could not rise. The middle one is a passive with no one named as pushing. KJV 'cast down' is fair, though it hides the violence of the root dāḥâ, to shove or thrust, as of a man pushed over a ledge (Ps 118:13, 140:5). Radak and Meiri note the odd vowel on dōḥû, of the kind found in Ps 72:20, and read it as a passive. KJV 'shall not be able to rise' turns a completed 'were not able' into a future. Radak sets this against the righteous of Prov 24:16, who fall seven times and rise; the wicked fall once and the verse closes on qûm, 'rise', the one thing they cannot do.

philological_notes.note: 'There', a place word. Ibn Ezra and Meiri compare it to 'then' (as in Job 35:12, 'there they cry out and he does not answer'), so it can point to a time as well as a place; Malbim takes it for the world to come. The psalm gives no antecedent, and the verse works best with the pointing left open.
A perfect ('they have fallen') about a fall still to come. Radak and Metzudat Zion call it a past form in place of the future, the usual way of speaking of what is certain.
'Doers of trouble', the committed wrongdoers, a stock phrase of the Psalms (5:6, 6:9, 14:4). 'Āwen covers harm, deceit and nothingness at once; 'iniquity' fits only part of it.

A passive 'they were pushed down' with an irregular vowel (holem for the expected qamets hatuf), compared by Radak and Meiri to kallû in Ps 72:20; the guttural het cannot take a dagesh, so the vowel changes. The root means a violent shove.
